Setup Instructions
The Pico needs to be connected to your computer through the USB cable for power (unless provided externally), to upload a program on it, and to communicate with it during the execution of the program (printing in a terminal or reading user input from keyboard).

title: Getting Started
text:
First binaries
Binaries are files that contain machine instructions for the Pico. The file extension is .uf2. When programming in C, such binary is produced on your computer and needs to be transfered to the Pico. When using micropython, the micropython interpreter is the binary that needs to be transfered to the Pico. After this, python programs can be transfered to it to be interpreted on the machine.
Here, we will follow the Your First Binaries section of the Pico tutorial to practice this step and test the Pico.
To load a program on the Pico, follow this process:

Starting from a board disconnect from the computer, press the BOOTSEL button and insert the USB connection to your computer at the same time.
The Pico should show up as a USB drive on your computer.
Copy the exectuable .uf2 file on this drive.
This should upload the program on the Pico and restart it automatically.



LED Blink
Download and install the Blink UF2 file. This file supports all Pico variants. If all goes well, you should see the integrated LED blink on your board.


USB Serial communication
Download and install the ‘Hello World’ UF2 file. This file should also supports all Pico variants. Once it is installed and running, open a Serial monitor and connect it to the port of the board. The default baud rate is 115200.


Programming environment
We recommend using Visual Studio Code for this project, both for C/C++ programming and for MicroPython.
There are extensions available that greatly facilitate the development of programs. These can normally be installed directly from the VS Code environment.

Pico-vscode
MicroPico



Example project

CMicroPython


Go ahead and start a new project from an example. On VS Code, click on the Pico icon, on the left pane. Click new C/C++ project from example. Select your architecture (e.g. Pico 2 W) and an example, for instance blink. Select the folder where it will save the files, and create the new project. If VS Code tells you that you are in restricted mode, click manage and select “in trusted folder”. Select the .c file and inspect it. The click again on the Pico icon and click compile project. This will create an executable .uf2 file in the build subfolder. Upload that one of the Pico to test the program.


First, you need to download and install the version of MicroPython for your device at the following documentation page. This is a uf2 file that needs to be upload as usual to the Pico.
In VS Code, click on the Pico icon on the left pane. Select new micropython project. Give a name to the project, select a location for the folder, and create the project. Open the .py file and inspect the code. Right click on the source file on the explorer and select run curent file on Pico to try it.

title: Interrupts
text:
Overview
There were two issues with the code we previously studied to toggle the state of an LED with a button.
The main issue was related to the debouncing - the fact that when a mechanical switch toggles, it doesn’t do it cleanly, but oscillates for a few milliseconds. Adding a wait command could help regulate this issue.
The second issue is about performance. The main loop spends lots of resources monitoring the state of a pin, just in case it changes. This is resource intensive for a task that is not very complicated for such a power chip. If only we could delegate these mundane tasks to specialised circuits. Well, we can! This is the domain of interrupts.
An interrupt is precisely a hardware feature that allows a microcontroller to react instantly to real-world events without constantly checking for them in a loop. For this, you register a special function, called an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR), callback or handler. That function is not directly called in your code. Instead, we tell the microcontroller that certain events, such as a voltage transition on a GPIO pin, should be monitored, and that the handler function needs to be called when this happens. As soon as the event is detected, the hardware then immediately pauses the main execution thread, jumps to run your interrupt handler function, and then seamlessly resumes your main program right where it left off. Because interrupts respond to events, they are well suited for detecting the press of a button.
Whether implemented in C using callbacks or in MicroPython via Pin.irq(), interrupts use dedicated hardware to monitor changes, enabling fast response and leaving your main loop free to handle other tasks, or simply sleep to conserve power.

title: GPIO
GPIO
GPIO
text:
General-Purpose Input/Output
General-Purpose Input/Output (GPIO) pins are the physical, software-configurable physical pins on a microcontroller that allow it to interact with the outside world. Each pin can be programmed on the fly as an input to read electrical signals from external components like buttons, sensors, or switches, or as an output to drive devices by sending high or low voltage signals to LEDs, relays, or motor controllers. In addition to operating as digital lines (on/off), GPIOs may also offer other advanced features, such as analog voltage readings (ADC), analog voltage outputs (DAC), or serve as hardware buses for standard communication protocols like I2C, SPI, and UART. They form the fundamental bridge between low-level software logic and hardware physics in embedded systems. This is why these pins need to be carefully configured at the start of any device programming applications based on the project requirements.
The microcontroller’s datasheet and pin layout are available on the Raspberry Pi website.



RP Pico 2 W pinout




Pull-down and pull-up resistors
When a GPIO pin is configured as a digital input, it voltage value is by definition not defined, and therefore needs to be controlled by the environment. If the pin isn’t actively connected to a solid voltage source (like 3.3V) or ground (0V), it is in a floating state, susceptible to electrostatic noise and electromagnetic interference, causing the pin’s voltage to drift unpredictably between high and low, leading to erratic readings.
To avoid this, it is common to connect the pin to either the ground or Vcc with a relatively large resistor, which are called pull-down or pull-up resistors, respectively. This ensures that the default state is well controlled. The circuit below introduces a pull-down resistor for this purpose. You will also notice that the microcontroller itself offers the possibility to connect the GPIO pin to either a pull-up or pull-down resistor, achieving the same outcome. The code examples will also make use of this feature, so that you could remove the physical resistor if you want to. Feel free to explore how this work in due course.

title: I2C & Temperature Sensors
text:
The sensor’s datasheet
For any device you wish to connect using I :sup:2 C, you will need to:

identify or set the device address;
configure the device if needed, by setting the value of different registers controlling the operation of the device;
read and send data to the device.

All this information can be found in the data sheet of the device you are planning to use. Make sure you check the availability of a good documentation before selecting a device.
We will work with a sensor produced by NXP, with a rather good documentation to support the work of the developer. The data sheet of the LM75 sensor you will use is available here.
This is daunting document! It probably contains many technical words you are not familiar with (yet). However, you don’t need to understand it all to get to use the device in your application. Have a quick scan through it at first. If you know what you are looking for, you will get this information out of it quickly enough afterwards.
Consult the data-sheet of the sensor to identify its I2C address. You’ll see that there is actually a range of address. How to set it? Your sensor is already soldered to a breakout board. Look at the back of the breakout board, and try to understand how to set the address of the device.
Most of the time, there will also be sample codes available to you online, or good AI models to get you started. But being able to understand the content of the datasheet ensures that you are able to appreciate the full feature set of your device and understand its limitations.

Device registers
Section 7.4 of the datasheet lists the four data registers present in the sensor (see table 5 in datasheet). A register is a small section of memory to store a few bytes of data that the device needs.

The configuration register controls the different modes of operation of the device; you can read or write on it, although you would most likely simply write on it to set the desired behaviour of the sensor. Each bit of the register controls a certain behaviour of the sensor.
The temp register contains the last temperature reading; it is read only, as expected.
The other two registers contain the information needed to control the threshold temperatures, and will be further discussed in the next section of the tutorial.

All interactions with the device involve writing and reading the content of these registers, so this is what we will look at next.


Reading and writing on the registers
Each register has an address. There is a special register in the device called pointer register that sets which data register will be involved in the following reading or writing operation. We do not need to worry too much about the details, as communications will be handled by special functions in the mbed I2C library. But it is important to understand the sequence of typical I2C communications to be able to use properly these high level functions.
A typical sequence to write in the data registers consists in sending through I2C the device address (7 bits and R/W bit set to W), followed by the value of the pointer register, to indicate which data register we want to write on, and the data to store on this register (see figs 7 and 11 in the datasheet).
To read, a similar process is followed, but two steps are needed (See figs 8 and 11 in the datasheet). First, we send to the I2C bus the device address (7 bits and R/W bit set to W), followed by the value of the pointer register to indicate what we would want to read. The microcontroller would then send another start signal. The next part involves sending again to the I2C bus the device address, but this time with the R/W bit set to R. The master (microcontroller) would continue to control the clock, but this time the slave (sensor) would control the data line, and send, one byte at a time, the data requested.

title: PWM, H-Bridges & Temperature Control
text:
Pulse-Width-Modulation and LED brightness

What is Pulse-Width-Modulation ?
Pulse-width-modulation (PWM) is probably the most common way to produce an average analog voltage in electrical circuits via fast switching. The idea is simple: if you switch the voltage of a circuit between ON (Vcc volts) and OFF (0 volts) sufficiently fast, you will generate an average response in the circuit proportional to the ratio between the length of time the circuit was ON and overall period of the signal. This ratio is called the duty ratio.
Not all circuits will respond well to such perturbation. To deliver a smooth response, some local time average is required. If we drive an LED at 10kHz, the component can really switch on and off at this rate, but the eye only perceives the time average of the light emitted, as our response time is of the order of 10s of milliseconds. So this is very effective at creating the illusion of diming the light. In other situation, a low pass filter with a resistor and capacitor can provide the averaging, delivering an output voltage increasing with the duty ratio, as a primitive digital-analog converter.



Duty_cycle_PWM


This technique is so popular that you can find a full page on Wikipedia dedicated to it and several tutorials available on internet from Arduino and Sparkfun. You may find this video useful:

title: PWM, H-Bridges & Temperature Control
text:
Power electronics with a H-bridge

What is a H-bridge?
Microcontrollers are logical devices that function with very modest power. They are not very good at driving loads, like actuators, which typically require power at their inputs. The problem can be solved through an interface capable of injecting power to the actuator as a function of the logical signals of the microcontroller. This is the role of a H-bridge.
A H-bridge is a simple device. It is just a switching circuit connected to a large power generator, as shown in the figure below. The four switches S1-S4 route power to the load, represented in the figure by an encircled M (a motor, in this example).



H bridge. Source: Wikipedia


The switches are typically controlled by the microcontroller.

If S1 and S4 are closed, and S2 and S3 are open, a positive voltage is applied to the left side of the load (the motor spins in one direction).
If S2 and S3 are closed, and S1 and S4 are open, a positive voltage is applied to the right side of the load (the motor spins in the other direction).
If S1 and S3 are closed, and S2 and S4 are open, the same voltage is applied to both sides of the load (the motor does not want to move). The same happens if S2 and S4 are closed, and S1 and S3 are open.
If either S1 and S2 are closed, or S3 and S4 are closed, the generator is short circuited and terrible things will happen…

So, by using a H-bridge, you can apply a voltage to your load without strong restrictions on the amount of power. Selecting the configuration of the four switches S1-S4 (ON/OFF) you can also decide the direction of the driving voltage to the load. Finally, to modulate the intensity of the voltage, just use PWM, opening and closing S1-S4 at high frequency to generate a suitable average voltage.


L298N Driver
The L298N driver is a dual H-bridge that can be used with voltages between 3.2 V to 40 V and can supply up to 2 A per bridge. To know more about this driver, consults the relevant data-sheet from manufacturers of the driver integrated circuit and the manufacturer of the breakout board.
The image below, from the breakout board datasheet, shows the different inputs and outputs of the circuit.



L298N H bridge connections



Connect an external DC power supply to the ground and +12V Power pins terminal. The power voltage doesn’t need to be 12 V. Any value from 3.2 V to 40 V would work. This power must not be taken from the microcontroller itself. Pay attention to NOT reverse polarity.
Here, we will use only one of the two H-bridges. The load will be connected to the Output A terminals.
The pins IN1 and IN2 control the switches of the bridge and should be connected to digital outputs of your microcontroller. They would work with both 3.3 V and 5 V logic.

if IN1 and IN2 are at the same voltage (0 or 3.3 V), then there is no current through the load;
if IN1 = 1 and IN2 = 0, the current will flow in a certain direction through the load;
if IN1 = 0 and IN2 = 1, the current will flow in the opposite direction through the load;

The pin “A Enable” could be either set to 1 permanently using the jumper, or connected to a PWM input to modulate the load. In the example below, we will use PWM so the jumper needs to be removed and safely stored.
the +5V Power pin is not required here. It may be used to actually power the microcontroller, but we use here the USB connection to the computer to deliver power.
However, the microcontroller and the L298N H-bridge need to have the same ground. It is therefore important to connect the Power GND terminal of the H-bridge to a GND pin of the microcontroller.
